title: Timers: setTimeout, setInterval, and what "zero" really means

videos.script:
setTimeout looks like the simplest function in the language. {{simple}} Run this, in three hundred milliseconds. Most people read that as a promise about time. It is not one.

{{minimum}} The delay is a minimum. The callback joins the queue when the time is up, and it runs when the event loop gets to it, which can be much later if the page is busy. You will measure that today.

{{zero}} Then the question in the lesson's title: what zero really means. Zero is not now. It is after everything that is running, after every microtask, and, if you nest timers deeply enough, after a few milliseconds the browser adds on purpose.

{{interval}} setInterval repeats, and it has a habit of running callbacks back to back when the work takes longer than the gap. A setTimeout that schedules itself again does not.

{{debounce}} And the most useful timer pattern there is: waiting until someone has stopped typing before you search, so a word typed in seven keystrokes costs one request instead of seven.
